extended_example.Rmd

Basic Hawkes model

Univariate Hawkes process 

library(emhawkes)

This section shows how to specify, simulate, and fit a univariate Hawkes model. First, create an hspec object to define the model. The S4 class hspec includes slots such as mu, alpha, beta, dimens, rmark, and impact.

In a univariate model, mu, alpha, and beta can be supplied as numeric values, which are converted to matrices. The following example defines an unmarked univariate Hawkes model.

mu1 <- 0.3; alpha1 <- 1.2; beta1 <- 1.5
hspec1 <- new("hspec", mu = mu1, alpha = alpha1, beta = beta1)
show(hspec1)
#> An object of class "hspec" of 1-dimensional Hawkes process
#> 
#> Slot mu: 
#>      [,1]
#> [1,]  0.3
#> 
#> Slot alpha: 
#>      [,1]
#> [1,]  1.2
#> 
#> Slot beta: 
#>      [,1]
#> [1,]  1.5

The hsim function simulates a path from an hspec object. The size argument specifies the number of rows, including the initial state. The optional arguments lambda_component0 and N0 specify the initial intensity components and event counts, respectively. The intensity of the basic univariate Hawkes model is

λ(t)=μ+∫−∞tαe−β(t−s)dN(s)=μ+λc(0)e−βt+∫0tαe−β(t−s)dN(s) \lambda(t) = \mu + \int_{-\infty}^t \alpha e^{-\beta (t-s)} d N(s) = \mu + \lambda_c(0) e^{-\beta t} + \int_0^t \alpha e^{-\beta (t-s)} d N(s)

where lambda_component0 denotes

λc(0)=∫−∞0αeβsdN(s). \lambda_c(0) = \int_{-\infty}^0 \alpha e^{\beta s} d N(s).

If lambda_component0 is omitted, the function determines the initial intensity components internally. For a sufficiently long simulation of a stable model, the effect of the initial intensity diminishes over time. The default initial value of the counting process, N0, is zero.

set.seed(1107)
res1 <- hsim(hspec1, size = 1000)
summary(res1)
#> -------------------------------------------------------
#> Simulation result of exponential (marked) Hawkes model.
#> Realized path :
#>        arrival N1 mark lambda1
#>  [1,]  0.00000  0    0 0.90000
#>  [2,]  0.97794  1    1 0.43838
#>  [3,]  1.09001  2    1 1.43128
#>  [4,]  1.28999  3    1 2.02711
#>  [5,]  1.53225  4    1 2.33527
#>  [6,]  1.65001  5    1 3.01139
#>  [7,]  2.51807  6    1 1.36377
#>  [8,]  2.81710  7    1 1.74553
#>  [9,]  2.87547  8    1 2.72378
#> [10,]  3.16415  9    1 2.65016
#> [11,]  3.51378 10    1 2.40131
#> [12,]  4.22355 11    1 1.43843
#> [13,] 16.96752 12    1 0.30000
#> [14,] 17.71654 13    1 0.69015
#> [15,] 19.10293 14    1 0.49874
#> [16,] 24.06354 15    1 0.30082
#> [17,] 24.09256 16    1 1.44967
#> [18,] 28.40173 17    1 0.30366
#> [19,] 28.53743 18    1 1.28198
#> [20,] 28.56702 19    1 2.38725
#> ... with 980 more rows 
#> -------------------------------------------------------

The hsim function returns an S3 object of class hreal with the following components.

  • hspec is the model specification.

  • inter_arrival contains the times between consecutive events.

  • arrival is the cumulative sum of inter_arrival.

  • type identifies the counting process associated with each event: type ii corresponds to NiN_i.

  • mark contains the mark associated with each event.

  • N contains the cumulative event counts for each type.

  • Nc contains the cumulative marks for each type.

  • lambda contains the intensity immediately before each event.

  • rambda contains the intensity immediately after each event.

  • lambda_component and rambda_component contain the intensity components λij\lambda_{ij} immediately before and after each event, respectively.

With the default initial values, inter_arrival, type, mark, N, and Nc begin with zero. The summary() function displays the first 20 rows of the realized path by default. The print() function also displays the model specification and intensity components.

In this univariate model, lambda == mu + lambda_component.

# The first and third columns are equal.
cbind(res1$lambda[1:5], res1$lambda_component[1:5], mu1 + res1$lambda_component[1:5])
#>          [,1]     [,2]     [,3]
#> [1,] 0.900000 0.600000 0.900000
#> [2,] 0.438383 0.138383 0.438383
#> [3,] 1.431282 1.131282 1.431282
#> [4,] 2.027111 1.727111 2.027111
#> [5,] 2.335269 2.035269 2.335269

For all rows except the first, rambda equals lambda + alpha in this model.

# The second and third columns are equal except in the initial row.
cbind(res1$lambda[1:5], res1$rambda[1:5], res1$lambda[1:5] + alpha1)
#>          [,1]     [,2]     [,3]
#> [1,] 0.900000 0.900000 2.100000
#> [2,] 0.438383 1.638383 1.638383
#> [3,] 1.431282 2.631282 2.631282
#> [4,] 2.027111 3.227111 3.227111
#> [5,] 2.335269 3.535269 3.535269

The following calculation verifies the exponential decay between events.

# By definition, the following two are equal:
res1$lambda[2:6]
#> [1] 0.438383 1.431282 2.027111 2.335269 3.011391
mu1 + (res1$rambda[1:5] - mu1) * exp(-beta1 * res1$inter_arrival[2:6])
#> [1] 0.438383 1.431282 2.027111 2.335269 3.011391

Use logLik to evaluate the log-likelihood from the model specification and observed inter-arrival times.

logLik(hspec1, inter_arrival = res1$inter_arrival)
#> The initial values for intensity processes are not provided. Internally determined initial values are used.
#> loglikelihood 
#>     -214.2385

Use hfit for maximum likelihood estimation. The hspec0 object supplies the initial parameter values for optimization. For this univariate model, inter_arrival is the only required data argument. If the initial intensity component is known, pass it as lambda_component0; otherwise, the function determines it internally. The default optimization method is BFGS.

# Initial parameter values for numerical optimization.
mu0 <- 0.5; alpha0 <- 1.0; beta0 <- 1.8
hspec0 <- new("hspec", mu = mu0, alpha = alpha0, beta = beta0)
# Supply the initial values through hspec0.
mle <- hfit(hspec0, inter_arrival = res1$inter_arrival)
summary(mle)
#> --------------------------------------------
#> Maximum Likelihood estimation
#> BFGS maximization, 24 iterations
#> Return code 0: successful convergence 
#> Log-Likelihood: -213.4658 
#> 3  free parameters
#> Estimates:
#>        Estimate Std. error t value Pr(> t)    
#> mu1     0.33641    0.03486   9.651  <2e-16 ***
#> alpha1  1.16654    0.09480  12.305  <2e-16 ***
#> beta1   1.52270    0.12323  12.357  <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> --------------------------------------------

Use fitted_hspec() to reconstruct the model with the estimated parameters. By default, hfit() uses the final Hessian and standard errors from maxLik. Additional stabilization is optional. Request final_hessian = "stable" to check numerical Hawkes curvature across scaled difference steps without changing the optimizer’s estimates. For this requested calculation, summary() uses the checked covariance and NA standard errors indicate failed checks.

mle_checked <- hfit(hspec0, inter_arrival = res1$inter_arrival,
                    final_hessian = "stable")
fit_diagnostics(mle_checked)[c("status", "scaled_condition", "newton_decrement")]
#> $status
#> [1] "ok"
#> 
#> $scaled_condition
#> [1] 20.3342
#> 
#> $newton_decrement
#> [1] 0.001305333

A stable Hessian does not establish reliable confidence intervals. Check convergence, score, and multiple starting values. The fit retains its original parameter map, including shared parameters and fixed constants in component functions. fit_initial_state() retrieves the initial counts and initial intensity setting.

estimated <- fitted_hspec(mle)
initial <- fit_initial_state(mle)
inferred <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = estimated,
  inter_arrival = res1$inter_arrival, infer = TRUE), initial))
c(fitted = as.numeric(logLik(mle)), restored = inferred$loglikelihood)
#>    fitted  restored 
#> -213.4658 -213.4658
head(inferred$lambda)
#>        lambda1
#> [1,] 0.8873272
#> [2,] 0.4606831
#> [3,] 1.4247076
#> [4,] 1.9993195
#> [5,] 2.2929804
#> [6,] 2.9468134
head(inferred$res_process1)
#> [1] 0.1706982 0.4560080 0.6547397 0.3763245 2.1110149 0.6227413

When the initial intensity was omitted, its saved setting remains NULL and is recalculated using the restored parameters. The restored specification also retains the mark and residual generators for subsequent simulation.

Pass the restored model and initial-state arguments to hsim() to generate a new path. These arguments describe the start of the fitted observation window. They do not continue the path after its last event. Check the fit’s convergence and the model’s suitability for simulation first.

set.seed(1108)
simulated <- do.call(hsim, c(list(object = estimated, size = 100), initial))
head(simulated$arrival)
#> [1] 0.000000 1.434237 1.782855 3.231614 3.984735 4.465780

The saved fit retains the information needed to reconstruct the model later. Keep the observed data separately when re-evaluating the likelihood.

saveRDS(mle, "hawkes-fit.rds")
saved_fit <- readRDS("hawkes-fit.rds")
estimated <- fitted_hspec(saved_fit)
initial <- fit_initial_state(saved_fit)

Bivariate Hawkes model

The intensity process of a basic bivariate Hawkes model is defined by

λ1(t)=μ1+∫−∞tα11e−β11(t−s)dN1(s)+∫−∞tα12e−β12(t−s)dN2(s), \lambda_1(t) = \mu_1 + \int_{-\infty}^t \alpha_{11} e^{-\beta_{11}(t-s)} d N_1(s) + \int_{-\infty}^t \alpha_{12} e^{-\beta_{12}(t-s)} d N_2(s),

λ2(t)=μ2+∫−∞tα21e−β21(t−s)dN1(s)+∫−∞tα22e−β22(t−s)dN2(s). \lambda_2(t) = \mu_2 + \int_{-\infty}^t \alpha_{21} e^{-\beta_{21}(t-s)} d N_1(s) + \int_{-\infty}^t \alpha_{22} e^{-\beta_{22}(t-s)} d N_2(s).

For this bivariate model, mu is a 2-by-1 matrix, and alpha and beta are 2-by-2 matrices.

μ=[μ1μ2],α=[α11α12α21α22],β=[β11β12β21β22] \mu = \begin{bmatrix} \mu_1 \\ \mu_2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \alpha = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha_{11} & \alpha_{12} \\ \alpha_{21} & \alpha_{22} \end{bmatrix}, \quad \beta = \begin{bmatrix} \beta_{11} & \beta_{12} \\ \beta_{21} & \beta_{22} \end{bmatrix}

rmark generates marks during simulation and can be omitted for unmarked models. The 2-by-2 matrix lambda_component0 specifies the initial values of lambda11, lambda12, lambda21, and lambda22. The intensity processes are represented by

λ1(t)=μ1+λ11(t)+λ12(t), \lambda_1(t) = \mu_1 + \lambda_{11}(t) + \lambda_{12}(t),

λ2(t)=μ2+λ21(t)+λ22(t). \lambda_2(t) = \mu_2 + \lambda_{21}(t) + \lambda_{22}(t).

The terms λij\lambda_{ij} are called intensity components, and lambda_component0 specifies their initial values λij(0)\lambda_{ij}(0). If lambda_component0 is omitted, the function determines these values internally.

mu2 <- matrix(c(0.2), nrow = 2)
alpha2 <- matrix(c(0.5, 0.9, 0.9, 0.5), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
beta2 <- matrix(c(2.25, 2.25, 2.25, 2.25), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
hspec2 <- new("hspec", mu=mu2, alpha=alpha2, beta=beta2)
print(hspec2)
#> An object of class "hspec" of 2-dimensional Hawkes process
#> 
#> Slot mu: 
#>      [,1]
#> [1,]  0.2
#> [2,]  0.2
#> 
#> Slot alpha: 
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]  0.5  0.9
#> [2,]  0.9  0.5
#> 
#> Slot beta: 
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,] 2.25 2.25
#> [2,] 2.25 2.25

Use hsim to simulate the model.

set.seed(1107)
res2 <- hsim(hspec2,  size=1000)
summary(res2)
#> -------------------------------------------------------
#> Simulation result of exponential (marked) Hawkes model.
#> Realized path :
#>       arrival N1 N2 mark lambda1 lambda2
#>  [1,] 0.00000  0  0    0 0.52941 0.52941
#>  [2,] 0.57028  1  0    1 0.29130 0.29130
#>  [3,] 1.66175  1  1    1 0.25073 0.28505
#>  [4,] 2.17979  1  2    1 0.49638 0.38238
#>  [5,] 2.47685  1  3    1 0.81319 0.54975
#>  [6,] 2.64001  2  3    1 1.24825 0.78866
#>  [7,] 2.70249  3  3    1 1.54519 1.49341
#>  [8,] 2.94547  4  3    1 1.26810 1.46968
#>  [9,] 3.39313  4  4    1 0.77271 0.99242
#> [10,] 3.52533  4  5    1 1.29379 1.15989
#> [11,] 3.56971  5  5    1 2.00432 1.52115
#> [12,] 3.70761  5  6    1 1.88965 1.82866
#> [13,] 4.30122  5  7    1 0.88106 0.75983
#> [14,] 4.34337  6  7    1 1.63800 1.16393
#> [15,] 4.40222  7  7    1 1.89764 1.83275
#> [16,] 4.58943  8  7    1 1.64219 1.86211
#> [17,] 5.14665  9  7    1 0.75437 0.93131
#> [18,] 5.18186  9  8    1 1.17407 1.70707
#> [19,] 5.36167  9  9    1 1.45050 1.53925
#> [20,] 5.89118 10  9    1 0.85331 0.75875
#> ... with 980 more rows 
#> -------------------------------------------------------

In multivariate models, type identifies the counting process associated with each event.

# A bivariate model has two event types: 1 and 2.
res2$type[1:10]
#>  [1] 0 1 2 2 2 1 1 1 2 2

In multivariate models, the column names of N are N1, N2, N3, and so on.

res2$N[1:3, ]
#>      N1 N2
#> [1,]  0  0
#> [2,]  1  0
#> [3,]  1  1

Similarly, the column names of lambda are lambda1, lambda2, lambda3, and so on.

res2$lambda[1:3, ]
#>        lambda1   lambda2
#> [1,] 0.5294118 0.5294118
#> [2,] 0.2913028 0.2913028
#> [3,] 0.2507301 0.2850475

In this bivariate model, the columns of lambda_component are lambda11, lambda12, lambda21, and lambda22.

res2$lambda_component[1:3, ]
#>        lambda11    lambda12   lambda21    lambda22
#> [1,] 0.11764706 0.211764706 0.21176471 0.117647059
#> [2,] 0.03260813 0.058694641 0.05869464 0.032608134
#> [3,] 0.04569443 0.005035631 0.08224997 0.002797573

By definition, the following two expressions are equivalent:

mu2[1] + rowSums(res2$lambda_component[1:5, c("lambda11", "lambda12")])
#> [1] 0.5294118 0.2913028 0.2507301 0.4963769 0.8131889
res2$lambda[1:5, "lambda1"]
#> [1] 0.5294118 0.2913028 0.2507301 0.4963769 0.8131889

Extract the observed inter_arrival and type vectors from the simulation result. Both are required to fit a bivariate model.

inter_arrival2 <- res2$inter_arrival
type2 <- res2$type

Use logLik to evaluate the log-likelihood.

logLik(hspec2, inter_arrival = inter_arrival2, type = type2)
#> The initial values for intensity processes are not provided. Internally determined initial values are used.
#> loglikelihood 
#>     -974.2809

Use hfit to estimate the parameters from inter_arrival and type. The values of mu, alpha, and beta in hspec0 provide starting points for optimization. Here, we use the simulation parameters by setting hspec0 <- hspec2. For observed data, choose initial values because the true parameters are unknown.

The default fit groups equal starting values within each matrix and estimates four parameters here: one for mu, two for alpha, and one for beta. hfit explains this rule once before optimization.

hspec0 <- hspec2
mle <- hfit(hspec0, inter_arrival = inter_arrival2, type = type2)
#> hfit: equal starting values within each matrix share a parameter (reduced = TRUE; mu, alpha, beta).
#> Use reduced = FALSE to estimate matrix entries separately.
summary(mle)
#> --------------------------------------------
#> Maximum Likelihood estimation
#> BFGS maximization, 33 iterations
#> Return code 0: successful convergence 
#> Log-Likelihood: -970.1408 
#> 4  free parameters
#> Estimates:
#>          Estimate Std. error t value  Pr(> t)    
#> mu1       0.19095    0.01638  11.656  < 2e-16 ***
#> alpha1.1  0.48217    0.07430   6.489 8.64e-11 ***
#> alpha1.2  0.98625    0.09576  10.300  < 2e-16 ***
#> beta1.1   2.07987    0.17203  12.091  < 2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> --------------------------------------------
coef(mle)
#>       mu1  alpha1.1  alpha1.2   beta1.1 
#> 0.1909541 0.4821725 0.9862541 2.0798690
miscTools::stdEr(mle)
#>        mu1   alpha1.1   alpha1.2    beta1.1 
#> 0.01638200 0.07430500 0.09575744 0.17202504

The restored matrices retain the shared parameters from this fit. The diagonal entries of alpha remain equal, as do its off-diagonal entries.

estimated2 <- fitted_hspec(mle)
estimated2@alpha
#>           [,1]      [,2]
#> [1,] 0.4821725 0.9862541
#> [2,] 0.9862541 0.4821725
estimated2@beta
#>          [,1]     [,2]
#> [1,] 2.079869 2.079869
#> [2,] 2.079869 2.079869

Parameter settings

The initial values in hspec0 determine which parameters are estimated separately. With the default setting reduced = TRUE, equal entries within a parameter matrix share one estimated value. The rule is applied separately to each matrix; equal values in mu and alpha do not link those components. The startup message lists the matrices with shared entries. Use suppressMessages(hfit(...)) to hide it.

For example, if alpha[1,1] and alpha[1,2] have different initial values, hfit estimates them separately. If they have the same initial value, hfit treats them as a single parameter.

The previous example uses a symmetric Hawkes model: alpha is symmetric, and all entries of beta are equal.

print(hspec2)
#> An object of class "hspec" of 2-dimensional Hawkes process
#> 
#> Slot mu: 
#>      [,1]
#> [1,]  0.2
#> [2,]  0.2
#> 
#> Slot alpha: 
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]  0.5  0.9
#> [2,]  0.9  0.5
#> 
#> Slot beta: 
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,] 2.25 2.25
#> [2,] 2.25 2.25
set.seed(1107)
res2 <- hsim(hspec2, size = 1000)

In the first example, all entries of alpha0 are set to 0.75. This constrains alpha11, alpha12, alpha21, and alpha22 to share one estimated value, even though their simulation values differ. The same rule applies within mu0 and beta0.

mu0 <- matrix(c(0.15, 0.15), nrow = 2)
alpha0 <- matrix(c(0.75, 0.75, 0.75, 0.75), nrow = 2, byrow=TRUE)
beta0 <- matrix(c(2.6, 2.6, 2.6, 2.6), nrow = 2, byrow=TRUE)

hspec0 <- new("hspec", mu=mu0, alpha=alpha0, beta=beta0)
summary(hfit(hspec0, inter_arrival = res2$inter_arrival, type = res2$type))
#> hfit: equal starting values within each matrix share a parameter (reduced = TRUE; mu, alpha, beta).
#> Use reduced = FALSE to estimate matrix entries separately.
#> --------------------------------------------
#> Maximum Likelihood estimation
#> BFGS maximization, 46 iterations
#> Return code 0: successful convergence 
#> Log-Likelihood: -979.5687 
#> 3  free parameters
#> Estimates:
#>          Estimate Std. error t value Pr(> t)    
#> mu1       0.19125    0.01633   11.71  <2e-16 ***
#> alpha1.1  0.73981    0.05783   12.79  <2e-16 ***
#> beta1.1   2.09707    0.15936   13.16  <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> --------------------------------------------

This fit estimates one excitation parameter for both self-excitation and mutual excitation, whose simulation values are 0.5 and 0.9, respectively.

In the second example, alpha0 has the same symmetry as the simulation model. Its diagonal entries are equal, and its off-diagonal entries share a different value. The model therefore has two excitation parameters to estimate.

mu0 <- matrix(c(0.15, 0.15), nrow = 2)
alpha0 <- matrix(c(0.75, 0.751, 0.751, 0.75), nrow = 2, byrow=TRUE)
beta0 <- matrix(c(2.6, 2.6, 2.6, 2.6), nrow = 2, byrow=TRUE)

hspec0 <- new("hspec", mu=mu0, alpha=alpha0, beta=beta0)
summary(hfit(hspec0, inter_arrival = res2$inter_arrival, type = res2$type))
#> hfit: equal starting values within each matrix share a parameter (reduced = TRUE; mu, alpha, beta).
#> Use reduced = FALSE to estimate matrix entries separately.
#> --------------------------------------------
#> Maximum Likelihood estimation
#> BFGS maximization, 30 iterations
#> Return code 0: successful convergence 
#> Log-Likelihood: -970.1408 
#> 4  free parameters
#> Estimates:
#>          Estimate Std. error t value  Pr(> t)    
#> mu1       0.19095    0.01639  11.647  < 2e-16 ***
#> alpha1.1  0.48226    0.07292   6.614 3.74e-11 ***
#> alpha1.2  0.98626    0.09287  10.620  < 2e-16 ***
#> beta1.1   2.08008    0.16593  12.536  < 2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> --------------------------------------------

The third example allows mu1 and mu2 to differ, even though they are equal in the simulation model.

mu0 <- matrix(c(0.15, 0.14), nrow = 2)
alpha0 <- matrix(c(0.75, 0.751, 0.751, 0.75), nrow = 2, byrow=TRUE)
beta0 <- matrix(c(2.6, 2.6, 2.6, 2.6), nrow = 2, byrow=TRUE)

hspec0 <- new("hspec", mu=mu0, alpha=alpha0, beta=beta0)
summary(hfit(hspec0, inter_arrival = res2$inter_arrival, type = res2$type))
#> hfit: equal starting values within each matrix share a parameter (reduced = TRUE; alpha, beta).
#> Use reduced = FALSE to estimate matrix entries separately.
#> --------------------------------------------
#> Maximum Likelihood estimation
#> BFGS maximization, 42 iterations
#> Return code 0: successful convergence 
#> Log-Likelihood: -969.9914 
#> 5  free parameters
#> Estimates:
#>          Estimate Std. error t value Pr(> t)    
#> mu1       0.18300    0.02157   8.484  <2e-16 ***
#> mu2       0.19872    0.02206   9.006  <2e-16 ***
#> alpha1.1  0.48149    0.07569   6.361   2e-10 ***
#> alpha1.2  0.98720    0.09852  10.020  <2e-16 ***
#> beta1.1   2.07973    0.17931  11.598  <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> --------------------------------------------

Set reduced = FALSE to estimate each matrix entry separately, including entries with equal initial values.

summary(hfit(hspec2, inter_arrival = res2$inter_arrival, type = res2$type, reduced=FALSE))
#> hfit: some standard errors are NaN. Try final_hessian = "stable" for Hawkes Hessian stabilization.
#> --------------------------------------------
#> Maximum Likelihood estimation
#> BFGS maximization, 51 iterations
#> Return code 0: successful convergence 
#> Log-Likelihood: -966.5055 
#> 10  free parameters
#> Estimates:
#>          Estimate Std. error t value  Pr(> t)    
#> mu1       0.17997    0.02231   8.066 7.24e-16 ***
#> mu2       0.20060    0.02335   8.590  < 2e-16 ***
#> alpha1.1  0.44726    0.10661   4.195 2.73e-05 ***
#> alpha2.1  1.17743        NaN     NaN      NaN    
#> alpha1.2  0.97048    0.10742   9.035  < 2e-16 ***
#> alpha2.2  0.48979        NaN     NaN      NaN    
#> beta1.1   2.52210        NaN     NaN      NaN    
#> beta2.1   3.15498        NaN     NaN      NaN    
#> beta1.2   1.80167    0.07600  23.705  < 2e-16 ***
#> beta2.2   1.51338        NaN     NaN      NaN    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> --------------------------------------------

The same rules apply to higher-dimensional models. For function components, the named entries in param define the estimated parameters. Matching parameter names are shared across functions, even with reduced = FALSE. Use different names for independent parameters with equal starting values. Conflicting starting values for a shared name produce a warning, and the first value is used. A zero in a numeric matrix is an estimated starting value; constants inside a component function remain fixed.

Observed data and initial state

The first row is the initial state, followed by the observed events. For event times measured from the observation start, use c(0, diff(c(0, event_times))) for inter_arrival and prepend zero to the event-type and mark vectors. The likelihood currently ends at the last supplied event, and the input order is preserved when event times coincide.

N0 and Nc0 specify initial event counts and mark totals. Pass Nc0 by name in hfit. Use the same initial counts and lambda_component0 for simulation and likelihood evaluation when comparing their paths. A scalar lambda_component0 is expanded to all kernel components; a matrix must match the kernel dimensions. For multi-kernel models, supply lambda_component0 explicitly.

Counting-process matrices supplied as N or Nc must agree with the event data and initial counts. Each row contains the values after that event. A baseline function called with index n uses row n - 1 for the preceding state; an impact function uses row n for the current event. Component functions can declare only the arguments they need, and use ... to receive the remaining context.

Calculation engines

Numeric Hawkes specifications use the Rcpp engine automatically for likelihood evaluation and inference. During fitting, supported function components and impacts also use C++ automatically. Unsupported specifications and residual distributions use R. Standalone likelihood evaluation of function-valued models and simulation use R. Use the emhawkes.engine option to compare the R and automatic calculations. This function restores the previous option after each call.

engine_loglik <- function(engine) {
  previous <- options(emhawkes.engine = engine)
  on.exit(options(previous))
  as.numeric(logLik(hspec2, inter_arrival = inter_arrival2, type = type2))
}
c(R = engine_loglik("r"), automatic = engine_loglik("auto"))
#>         R automatic 
#> -974.2809 -974.2809

Residual process

Set infer = TRUE in logLik to obtain the log-likelihood, intensity paths, and residual processes. These are computed using the parameters in the supplied hspec object. For a univariate model, res_process1 contains the residual inter-arrival times.

hrp <- new("hspec", mu = 0.3, alpha = 1.2, beta = 1.5)
res_rp <- hsim(hrp, size = 1000)

# inferred result
infered_res <- logLik(hrp, res_rp$inter_arrival, infer = TRUE)

## QQ-plot
p <- ppoints(100)
q <- quantile(infered_res$res_process1, p = p)
plot(qexp(p), q, xlab="Theoretical Quantiles",ylab="Sample Quantiles")
qqline(q, distribution=qexp,col="blue", lty=2)

For observed data, estimate the parameters before computing the residual processes.


# estimation
mle_rp <- hfit(new("hspec", mu = 0.2, alpha = 1, beta = 2),
               res_rp$inter_arrival)

# Restore the estimated model and the initial-state arguments.
he <- fitted_hspec(mle_rp)
initial_rp <- fit_initial_state(mle_rp)

# infer intensity
infered_res <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = he,
  inter_arrival = res_rp$inter_arrival, type = res_rp$type, infer = TRUE), initial_rp))

rpe <- infered_res$res_process1

p <- ppoints(100)
q <- quantile(rpe, p=p)
plot(qexp(p), q, xlab="Theoretical Quantiles",ylab="Sample Quantiles")
qqline(q, distribution=qexp,col="blue", lty=2)

For an nn-dimensional model, logLik returns one residual process for each event type. In the following bivariate example, these are infer_res2$res_process1 and infer_res2$res_process2.

hrp2 <- new("hspec", mu = rep(0.3, 2), 
           alpha = matrix(c(1.2, 1.5, 1.5, 1.2), nrow=2), 
           beta = matrix(rep(3, 4), nrow=2))
res_hrp2 <- hsim(hrp2, size = 2000)

infer_res2 <- logLik(hrp2, res_hrp2$inter_arrival, res_hrp2$type, infer = TRUE)

p <- ppoints(100)
q <- quantile(c(infer_res2$res_process1, infer_res2$res_process2), p=p)
plot(qexp(p), q, xlab="Theoretical Quantiles",ylab="Sample Quantiles")
qqline(q, distribution=qexp,col="blue", lty=2)

# Plot the pooled residuals for both event types.

hist(
  c(infer_res2$res_process1, infer_res2$res_process2),
  breaks = 50,
  probability = TRUE,
  main = "Histogram of Inferred Residual Process",
  xlab = "Residual Value",
  ylab = "Density"
)

x <- seq(0, 8, 0.1)

lines(
  x,
  dexp(x),
  col = 'red',
  lwd = 2
)

legend("topright", legend = "Theoretical PDF", col = "red", lwd = 2)

More complex models

Multi-kernel model

A multi-kernel Hawkes model requires type_col_map in its hspec object. This list maps each event type to the corresponding columns of the kernel parameter matrices. Consider a bivariate multi-kernel model:

λt=μ+∫−∞th(t−u)dN(u) \lambda_t = \mu + \int_{-\infty}^{t} h(t-u) d N(u)

where

h=∑k=1Khk,hk(t)=αk∘[e−βk11te−βk12te−βk21te−βk22t] h = \sum_{k=1}^{K} h_k, \quad h_k (t) = \alpha_k \circ \begin{bmatrix} e^{-\beta_{k11} t} & e^{-\beta_{k12} t} \\ e^{-\beta_{k21} t} & e^{-\beta_{k22} t} \end{bmatrix}

Here, kk indexes the kernels, αk\alpha_k is the excitation matrix for kernel kk, and ∘\circ denotes elementwise multiplication.

For a bivariate Hawkes model with two kernels, the intensity processes are

[λ1(t)λ2(t)]=[μ1μ2]+∫−∞t[α111e−β111(t−s)α112e−β112(t−s)α121e−β121(t−s)α122e−β122(t−s)][dN1(s)dN2(s)]+∫−∞t[α211e−β211(t−s)α212e−β212(t−s)α221e−β221(t−s)α222e−β222(t−s)][dN1(s)dN2(s)]. \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1(t) \\ \lambda_2(t) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mu_1 \\ \mu_2 \end{bmatrix} + \int_{-\infty}^{t} \begin{bmatrix} \alpha_{111} e^{-\beta_{111}(t-s)} & \alpha_{112} e^{-\beta_{112}(t-s)} \\ \alpha_{121}e^{-\beta_{121}(t-s)} & \alpha_{122}e^{-\beta_{122}(t-s)} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} d N_1(s) \\ dN_2(s) \end{bmatrix} + \int_{-\infty}^{t} \begin{bmatrix} \alpha_{211} e^{-\beta_{211}(t-s)} & \alpha_{212} e^{-\beta_{212}(t-s)} \\ \alpha_{221}e^{-\beta_{221}(t-s)} & \alpha_{222}e^{-\beta_{222}(t-s)} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} d N_1(s) \\ dN_2(s) \end{bmatrix}.

The parameter matrices are

α=[α111α112α211α212α121α122α221α222],β=[β111β112β211β212β121β122β221β222] \alpha = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha_{111} & \alpha_{112} & \alpha_{211} & \alpha_{212} \\ \alpha_{121} & \alpha_{122} & \alpha_{221} & \alpha_{222} \end{bmatrix}, \quad \beta = \begin{bmatrix} \beta_{111} & \beta_{112} & \beta_{211} & \beta_{212} \\ \beta_{121} & \beta_{122} & \beta_{221} & \beta_{222} \end{bmatrix} \quad

The mapping must specify which columns correspond to each counting process NiN_i.

mu <- matrix(c(0.02, 0.02), nrow=2)
      
beta_1 <- matrix(rep(10, 4), nrow=2) 
beta_2 <- matrix(rep(1, 4), nrow=2)
beta  <- cbind(beta_1, beta_2)
      
alpha_1 <- matrix(c(3, 2,
                    2, 3), nrow=2, byrow=TRUE)
alpha_2 <- matrix(c(0.3, 0.2,
                    0.2, 0.3), nrow=2, byrow=TRUE)
alpha <- cbind(alpha_1, alpha_2)

print(alpha)
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]    3    2  0.3  0.2
#> [2,]    2    3  0.2  0.3

The first and third columns of α\alpha correspond to N1N_1, and the second and fourth columns correspond to N2N_2. Thus, define type_col_map as follows:

type_col_map <- list(c(1,3),  # columns for dN1
                     c(2,4))  # columns for dN2
type_col_map
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1 3
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 2 4

The entry type_col_map[[i]] lists the columns associated with event type i. Rows of the intensity matrix identify event types. After a type i event, type_col_map[[i]] selects the kernel columns to update. Use this mapping to extract the corresponding parameters:

cat("Part of alpha associated with N1: \n")
#> Part of alpha associated with N1:
alpha[, type_col_map[[1]]]  # associated with N1
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    3  0.3
#> [2,]    2  0.2
cat("Part of alpha associated with N2: \n")
#> Part of alpha associated with N2:
alpha[, type_col_map[[2]]]  # associated with N2
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    2  0.2
#> [2,]    3  0.3

cat("Part of beta associated with N1: \n")
#> Part of beta associated with N1:
beta[, type_col_map[[1]]]  # associated with N1
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]   10    1
#> [2,]   10    1
cat("Part of beta associated with N2: \n")
#> Part of beta associated with N2:
beta[, type_col_map[[2]]]  # associated with N2
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]   10    1
#> [2,]   10    1
h <- new("hspec", mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta=beta, type_col_map = type_col_map)
h
#> An object of class "hspec" of 2-dimensional Hawkes process
#> 
#> Slot mu: 
#>      [,1]
#> [1,] 0.02
#> [2,] 0.02
#> 
#> Slot alpha: 
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]    3    2  0.3  0.2
#> [2,]    2    3  0.2  0.3
#> 
#> Slot beta: 
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]   10   10    1    1
#> [2,]   10   10    1    1
#> 
#> Slot type_col_map: 
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1 3
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 2 4

For this multi-kernel model, lambda_component0 must be supplied for both simulation and estimation.

set.seed(620)
lambda_component0_mk <- matrix(seq(1, 1.7, 0.1), nrow = 2)
res_mk <- hsim(h, size = 3000, lambda_component0 = lambda_component0_mk)

This example explicitly requests the checked final Hessian. The original estimate is retained, but its score calls for tighter optimization and multiple starting values. Kernel starting order and the fixed initial state can affect the selected local solution.

fit_diagnostics(fit_mk)[c("status", "newton_decrement", "warnings")]
#> $status
#> [1] "ok"
#> 
#> $newton_decrement
#> [1] 0.0003105941
#> 
#> $warnings
#> character(0)

Reconstruction retains type_col_map and the supplied initial intensity matrix. Each kernel uses its own decay rate in the likelihood and residual integrals. The inferred likelihood agrees with the fitted likelihood even though decay rates differ within each row.

estimated_mk <- fitted_hspec(fit_mk)
initial_mk <- fit_initial_state(fit_mk)
estimated_mk@type_col_map
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1 3
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 2 4
initial_mk$lambda_component0
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]  1.0  1.2  1.4  1.6
#> [2,]  1.1  1.3  1.5  1.7
inferred_mk <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = estimated_mk,
  inter_arrival = res_mk$inter_arrival, type = res_mk$type, infer = TRUE), initial_mk))
c(fitted = as.numeric(logLik(fit_mk)), restored = inferred_mk$loglikelihood)
#>   fitted restored 
#>  6084.72  6084.72
all.equal(as.numeric(logLik(fit_mk)), inferred_mk$loglikelihood)
#> [1] TRUE

Synchronized intensity model

This is a two-kernel model with the following reparameterization.

μ=[θ/(1−κ)/2+θ̃/(1+κ)/2θ/(1−κ)/2−θ̃/(1+κ)/2],θ=(θ−+θ+)/2,θ̃=(θ−−θ+)/2 \mu = \begin{bmatrix} \theta/(1 - \kappa)/2 + \tilde\theta/(1 + \kappa)/2 \\ \theta/(1 - \kappa)/2 - \tilde\theta/(1 + \kappa)/2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \theta = (\theta^- + \theta^+)/2,\quad \tilde\theta=(\theta^- -\theta^+)/2

α=[ζζ̃ζ−ζ̃ζ−ζ̃ζζ̃],ζ=(η+ν)/2,ζ̃=(η−ν)/2 \alpha = \begin{bmatrix} \zeta & \tilde\zeta & \zeta & -\tilde\zeta \\ \zeta & -\tilde\zeta & \zeta & \tilde\zeta \end{bmatrix}, \quad \zeta = (\eta + \nu) / 2, \quad \tilde \zeta = (\eta - \nu)/ 2

β=[β1β2β1β2β1β2β1β2],β1=β(1−κ),β2=β(1+κ) \beta = \begin{bmatrix} \beta_1 & \beta_2 & \beta_1 & \beta_2 \\ \beta_1 & \beta_2 & \beta_1 & \beta_2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \beta_1 = \beta(1 - \kappa), \quad \beta_2 = \beta(1 + \kappa)

To implement this reparameterization, define mu, alpha, and beta as functions. Each function takes a named parameter vector, param, as its first argument.

mu <- function(param = c(theta_p = 0.15, theta_n = 0.21, kappa = 0.12)){
  theta    <- (param["theta_n"] + param["theta_p"])/2
  theta_tl <- (param["theta_n"] - param["theta_p"])/2
  matrix(c(theta/2/(1 - param["kappa"]) + theta_tl/2/(1 + param["kappa"]),
           theta/2/(1 - param["kappa"]) - theta_tl/2/(1 + param["kappa"])), nrow=2)
}

alpha <- function(param = c(eta = 5, nu = 3)){
  zeta    <- (param["eta"] + param["nu"])/2
  zeta_tl <- (param["eta"] - param["nu"])/2
  matrix(c(zeta, zeta_tl, zeta, -zeta_tl,
           zeta, -zeta_tl, zeta, zeta_tl), nrow=2, byrow=TRUE)
}

beta <- function(param = c(beta = 12, kappa = 0.12)){
  beta1 <- param["beta"] * (1 - param["kappa"])
  beta2 <- param["beta"] * (1 + param["kappa"])
  matrix(c(beta1, beta2, beta1, beta2,
           beta1, beta2, beta1, beta2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
}

type_col_map <- list(c(1,2), c(3,4))

h_sy <- new("hspec", mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, type_col_map = type_col_map)
h_sy
#> An object of class "hspec" of 2-dimensional Hawkes process
#> 
#> Slot mu: 
#> function (param = c(theta_p = 0.15, theta_n = 0.21, kappa = 0.12)) 
#> {
#>     theta <- (param["theta_n"] + param["theta_p"])/2
#>     theta_tl <- (param["theta_n"] - param["theta_p"])/2
#>     matrix(c(theta/2/(1 - param["kappa"]) + theta_tl/2/(1 + param["kappa"]), 
#>         theta/2/(1 - param["kappa"]) - theta_tl/2/(1 + param["kappa"])), 
#>         nrow = 2)
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x5621179179c8>
#> 
#> Slot alpha: 
#> function (param = c(eta = 5, nu = 3)) 
#> {

#>     zeta_tl <- (param["eta"] - param["nu"])/2
#>     matrix(c(zeta, zeta_tl, zeta, -zeta_tl, zeta, -zeta_tl, zeta, 
#>         zeta_tl), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x562115bc92a0>
#> 
#> Slot beta: 
#> function (param = c(beta = 12, kappa = 0.12)) 
#> {
#>     beta1 <- param["beta"] * (1 - param["kappa"])
#>     beta2 <- param["beta"] * (1 + param["kappa"])
#>     matrix(c(beta1, beta2, beta1, beta2, beta1, beta2, beta1, 
#>         beta2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x5621160a4990>

# run simulation
res_sy <- hsim(h_sy, size = 2000, lambda_component0 = matrix(rep(1, 2 * 4), nrow=2))
summary(res_sy)

The parameters to estimate and their initial values are taken from the default param vectors. Parameters with the same name are shared across functions. For example, kappa appears in both mu and beta, but only one kappa is estimated.

fit_sy <- hfit(h_sy, inter_arrival=res_sy$inter_arrival,
               type=res_sy$type,
               lambda_component0 = matrix(rep(1, 2 * 4), nrow=2),
               final_hessian = "stable")
summary(fit_sy)

The restored component functions use the estimated defaults. Both functions retain the same estimated kappa.

estimated_sy <- fitted_hspec(fit_sy)
c(mu = eval(formals(estimated_sy@mu)$param)[["kappa"]],
  beta = eval(formals(estimated_sy@beta)$param)[["kappa"]])
#>        mu      beta 
#> 0.4099007 0.4099007

Extended models

The package supports the following family of extended multivariate marked Hawkes models:

λ(t)=μ+∫(−∞,t)×Eh(t,u,z)M(du×dz) \lambda(t) = \mu + \int_{(-\infty,t)\times E} h(t, u, z)M(du \times dz)

where the kernel hh is

h(t,u,z)=(α+g(t,z))Γ(t), h(t, u, z) = (\alpha + g(t, z))\Gamma(t),

The components are:

  • α\alpha is a constant matrix.

  • g(t,z)g(t, z) describes additional effects on the intensities and may depend on the mark or the history of the underlying processes.

  • Γ(t)\Gamma(t) is a matrix of exponential decay terms, with Γij(t)=e−βijt\Gamma_{ij}(t) = e^{-\beta_{ij}t}.

  • MM is a vector of random measures on the product of the time and mark spaces.

Linear impact model

In the linear impact model,

g(t,z)=η(z−1). g(t, z) = \eta (z-1).

The impact function represents g(t,z)g(t, z), the additional effect of a mark on future intensity. For details, see Marked Hawkes process modeling of price dynamics and volatility estimation.

Its first argument, param, contains the model parameters. Additional arguments, such as n and mark, provide information about the model or realized path. Include ... to accept other arguments supplied by the package. The rmark function generates marks during simulation.

mu <- matrix(c(0.15, 0.15), nrow=2)
alpha <- matrix(c(0.75, 0.6, 0.6, 0.75), nrow=2, byrow=T)
beta <- matrix(c(2.6, 2.6, 2.6, 2.6), nrow=2)
rmark <- function(param = c(p=0.65), ...){
  rgeom(1, p=param[1]) + 1
}

impact <- function(param = c(eta1=0.2), alpha, n, mark, ...){
  ma <- matrix(rep(mark[n]-1, 4), nrow = 2)
  ma * matrix( rep(param["eta1"], 4), nrow=2)
}

hi <- new("hspec", mu=mu, alpha=alpha, beta=beta,
          rmark = rmark,
          impact=impact)
hi

#>

For linear mark effects, specify the eta slot directly. The resulting intensity process is

λ(t)=μ+∫(−∞,t)×E(α+η(z−1))e−β(t−u)M(du×dz). \lambda(t) = \mu + \int_{(-\infty, t)\times E} (\alpha + \eta (z-1)) e^{-\beta(t-u)} M(du \times dz). 


rmark <- function(param = c(p=0.65), ...){
  rgeom(1, p=param[1]) + 1
}

h <-  new("hspec", mu=0.15, alpha=0.7, beta=1.6, eta=0.3,
          rmark = rmark)

To estimate the parameters of the mark distribution as well, supply its density or probability mass function in the dmark slot.

h_md <- h

h_md@dmark <- function(param = c(p = 0.1), n=n, mark=mark, ...){
   dgeom(mark[n] - 1, prob = param["p"])
}

mle_md <- hfit(h_md, 
               inter_arrival = res$inter_arrival, type = res$type, mark = res$mark)
summary(mle_md)
#> --------------------------------------------
#> Maximum Likelihood estimation
#> BFGS maximization, 45 iterations
#> Return code 0: successful convergence 
#> Log-Likelihood: -2657.079 
#> 5  free parameters
#> Estimates:

#> beta1  1.489843   0.126225  11.803 < 2e-16 ***
#> eta1   0.336259   0.076805   4.378 1.2e-05 ***
#> p      0.658970   0.012235  53.859 < 2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> --------------------------------------------

The density and generator use the same parameter name, p. Reconstruction updates rmark with the value estimated through dmark, so new simulations use the fitted mark distribution. Generator parameters that do not match estimated coefficient names keep their original defaults.

estimated_md <- fitted_hspec(mle_md)
c(density = eval(formals(estimated_md@dmark)$param)[["p"]],
  generator = eval(formals(estimated_md@rmark)$param)[["p"]])
#>   density generator 
#>   0.65897   0.65897

Hawkes flocking model

The function gg need not depend on the mark. In the Hawkes flocking model, the kernel components are α=[α11α1200α12α110000α33α3400α34α33], \alpha = \begin{bmatrix}\alpha_{11} & \alpha_{12} & 0 & 0 \\\alpha_{12}& \alpha_{11} & 0 & 0 \\0 & 0 & \alpha_{33} & \alpha_{34} \\0 & 0 & \alpha_{34} & \alpha_{33} \end{bmatrix}, g=[00α1w1{C1(t)<C2(t)}α1n1{C1(t)<C2(t)}00α1n1{C1(t)>C2(t)}α1w1{C1(t)>C2(t)}α2w1{C2(t)<C1(t)}α2n1{C2(t)<C1(t)}00α2n1{C2(t)>C1(t)}α2w1{C2(t)>C1(t)}00], g = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & \alpha_{1w} 1_{\{C_1(t) < C_2(t)\}} & \alpha_{1n} 1_{\{C_1(t) < C_2(t)\}} \\ 0 & 0 & \alpha_{1n} 1_{\{C_1(t) > C_2(t)\}} & \alpha_{1w}1_{\{C_1(t) > C_2(t)\}} \\ \alpha_{2w} 1_{\{C_2(t) < C_1(t)\}} & \alpha_{2n}1_{\{C_2(t) < C_1(t)\}} & 0 & 0 \\ \alpha_{2n} 1_{\{C_2(t) > C_1(t)\}} & \alpha_{2w}1_{\{C_2(t) > C_1(t)\}} & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix},

where

C1(t)=N1(t)−N2(t),C2(t)=N3(t)−N4(t). C_1(t) = N_1(t) - N_2(t), \quad C_2(t) = N_3(t) - N_4(t). For details, see Systemic risk in market microstructure of crude oil and gasoline futures prices: A Hawkes flocking model approach.

The alpha slot can contain a function that returns a matrix. In the following example, the function returns a 4×44\times4 matrix with some entries fixed at zero. Only the parameters in param are estimated. For simulation, a fixed matrix and a function returning the same matrix give the same model.

mu <- matrix(c(0.02, 0.02, 0.04, 0.04), nrow = 4)


alpha <- function(param = c(alpha11 = 0.2, alpha12 = 0.3, alpha33 = 0.3, alpha34 = 0.4)){
  matrix(c(param["alpha11"], param["alpha12"], 0, 0,
           param["alpha12"], param["alpha11"], 0, 0,
           0, 0, param["alpha33"], param["alpha34"],
           0, 0, param["alpha34"], param["alpha33"]), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)
}


beta <- matrix(c(rep(0.7, 8), rep(1.1, 8)), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)

The impact function below implements the model definition. Its N argument contains the counting process values, and n identifies the current event index. Include both arguments because the function uses them, along with ... to accept other arguments supplied by the package.

impact <- function(param = c(alpha1n=0.25, alpha1w=0.1, alpha2n=0.1, alpha2w=0.2),
                   N=N, n=n, ...){
  
  Psi <- matrix(c(0, 0, param['alpha1w'], param['alpha1n'],
                  0, 0, param['alpha1n'], param['alpha1w'],
                  param['alpha2w'], param['alpha2n'], 0, 0,
                  param['alpha2n'], param['alpha2w'], 0, 0), nrow=4, byrow=TRUE)
  
  ind <- N[,"N1"][n] - N[,"N2"][n] > N[,"N3"][n] - N[,"N4"][n]
  
  km <- matrix(c(!ind, !ind, !ind, !ind,
                 ind, ind, ind, ind,
                 ind, ind, ind, ind,
                 !ind, !ind, !ind, !ind), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)
  
  km * Psi
}

hspec_fl <- new("hspec",
                mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, impact = impact)
hspec_fl

This impact depends on observed event counts, so automatic selection uses the C++ likelihood with numerical differentiation. No Jacobian is needed; R still evaluates the impact.

previous_engine <- options(emhawkes.engine = "cpp")
fit_fl_cpp <- hfit(hspec_fl, hr_fl$inter_arrival, hr_fl$type)
options(previous_engine)

Bid-ask price model

This model describes bid and ask prices using a system of counting processes and their conditional intensities:

Nt=[N1(t)N2(t)N3(t)N4(t)],λt=[λ1(t)λ2(t)λ3(t)λ4(t)] N_t = \begin{bmatrix} N_1(t) \\ N_2(t) \\ N_3(t) \\ N_4(t) \end{bmatrix}, \quad \lambda_t = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1(t) \\ \lambda_2(t) \\ \lambda_3(t) \\ \lambda_4(t) \end{bmatrix}

In the unmarked case, the changes in ask and bid prices are N1(t)−N2(t)N_1(t) - N_2(t) and N3(t)−N4(t)N_3(t) - N_4(t), respectively. The marked example below uses Nc to accumulate price changes. The midprice p(t)p(t) is the average of the ask and bid prices, including their initial levels.

The base intensity process is

μ=[μ1ζℓ(t−)ζℓ(t−)μ1],ℓ(t)=L(t)p(t)\mu = \begin{bmatrix} \mu_1 \\ \zeta \ell(t-) \\ \zeta \ell(t-) \\ \mu_1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \ell(t) = \frac{L(t)}{p(t)}

where L(t)∈{0,1,2,…}L(t) \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\} measures the bid-ask spread above its minimum level, so L(t)=0L(t)=0 corresponds to the minimum spread. For details, see Modeling bid and ask price dynamics with an extended Hawkes process and its empirical applications for high-frequency stock market data.

In the mu function below, n identifies the current event index, and Nc is used to calculate the spread level and midprice.

# presumed initial bid and ask prices
initial_ask_price <- 1250 #cents
initial_bid_price <- 1150 #cents

initial_level <- round((initial_ask_price - initial_bid_price) - 1)
initial_mid_price <- (initial_bid_price + initial_ask_price) / 2

mu <- function(param = c(mu1 = 0.08, zeta1 = 0.10), n=n, Nc=Nc, ...){

  if(n == 1){
    
    level <- initial_level
    mid <- initial_mid_price
    
  } else {
    
    level <- Nc[n-1,1] - Nc[n-1,2] - (Nc[n-1,3] - Nc[n-1,4]) + initial_level
    ask <- initial_ask_price + (Nc[n-1,1] - Nc[n-1,2]) 
    bid <- initial_bid_price + (Nc[n-1,3] - Nc[n-1,4]) 
    mid <- (ask + bid) / 2
    
  }
  
  if(level <= 0){
    matrix(c(param["mu1"], 0,
             0, param["mu1"]), nrow = 4)
  } else {
    matrix(c(param["mu1"], param["zeta1"] * level / mid,
             param["zeta1"]*level / mid, param["mu1"]), nrow = 4)

  }

}

In addition, the kernel is represented by

h(t,u)=[αs1αmαs20αw1αn1(u)αn1(u)αw2αw2αn2(u)αn2(u)αw10αs2αmαs1],h(t, u) = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha_{s1} & \alpha_{m} & \alpha_{s2} & 0 \\ \alpha_{w1} & \alpha_{n1}(u) & \alpha_{n1}(u) & \alpha_{w2} \\ \alpha_{w2} & \alpha_{n2}(u) & \alpha_{n2}(u) & \alpha_{w1} \\ 0 & \alpha_{s2} & \alpha_{m} & \alpha_{s1} \\ \end{bmatrix},

where

αn1(u)=−∑j=14λ2j(u)+ξℓ(u),αn2(u)=−∑j=14λ3j(u)+ξℓ(u), \alpha_{n1}(u) = - \sum_{j=1}^4 \lambda_{2j}(u) + \xi \ell(u), \quad \alpha_{n2}(u) = - \sum_{j=1}^4 \lambda_{3j}(u) + \xi \ell(u),

Here, ξ≥0\xi \geq 0 is a constant, and λij\lambda_{ij} is a component of λi\lambda_i, defined by

λij(t)=∫−∞thij(t,u)dNj(u).\lambda_{ij}(t) = \int_{-\infty}^t h_{ij}(t, u) d N_j(u).

The following code places the constant part of hh in alpha and the state-dependent part in impact. The lambda_component_n argument supplies the current pre-jump matrix of λij\lambda_{ij} values. This avoids allocating a full intensity history when only the current state is needed. Individual components can be negative after a reset. The equal decay rates used here allow simulation as long as the sum of the components in each row remains nonnegative.


alpha <- function(param = c(alpha_s1=4, alpha_m=26, alpha_s2=5,
                            alpha_w1=11, alpha_w2=7)){
  matrix(c(param["alpha_s1"], param["alpha_m"], param["alpha_s2"], 0,
           param["alpha_w1"], 0, 0, param["alpha_w2"],
           param["alpha_w2"], 0, 0, param["alpha_w1"],
           0, param["alpha_s2"], param["alpha_m"], param["alpha_s1"]), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)
}

impact <- function(param = c(xi = 2.7), n=n, Nc=Nc, lambda_component_n = lambda_component_n, ... ){
  if(n == 1){
    level <-  initial_level
    # mid <- initial_mid_price
  } else {
    level <- Nc[n,1] - Nc[n,2] - (Nc[n,3] - Nc[n,4]) + initial_level
    ask <- initial_ask_price + (Nc[n,1] - Nc[n,2])
    bid <- initial_bid_price + (Nc[n,3] - Nc[n,4])
    mid <- (ask + bid)/2
  }
  
  lambda_component_matrix <- lambda_component_n

  l2 <- sum(lambda_component_matrix[2,]) # sum of second row
  l3 <- sum(lambda_component_matrix[3,]) # sum of third row

  im <- matrix(c(0, 0, 0, 0,
                 0, -l2 + param["xi"]*level/mid, -l2 + param["xi"]*level/mid, 0,
                 0, -l3 + param["xi"]*level/mid, -l3 + param["xi"]*level/mid, 0,
                 0, 0, 0, 0), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)

}

beta <- matrix(rep(50, 16), nrow = 4, byrow=TRUE)

rmark <- function(n=n, Nc=Nc, type, ...){
  if(n == 1){
    level <-  initial_level
  } else {
    level <- Nc[n-1,1] - Nc[n-1,2] - (Nc[n-1,3] - Nc[n-1,4]) + initial_level
  }
  if (type[n] == 2 | type[n] == 3){
    min(level,  rgeom(1, p=0.65) + 1)
  } else {
    rgeom(1, p=0.65) + 1
  }
}


h_ba <- new("hspec", mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, impact=impact, rmark = rmark)
h_ba

       mark = hr_ba$mark, Nc = hr_ba$Nc,
       lambda_component0 = matrix(rep(1, 16), 4))

Automatic selection uses the C++ likelihood for this observed baseline and sequential impact with numerical differentiation. The impact reads the current state before its jump. No Jacobian is required. The explicit engine setting below can be used to require C++ support.

previous_engine <- options(emhawkes.engine = "cpp")
mle_ba_cpp <- hfit(h_ba, hr_ba$inter_arrival, hr_ba$type, hr_ba$mark,
                   lambda_component0 = matrix(1, 4, 4),
                   final_hessian = "stable")
options(previous_engine)

Point processes with flexible residuals

One-dimensional model

The following example defines a point process with a custom residual distribution. For details, see Self and mutually exciting point process embedding flexible residuals and intensity with discretely Markovian dynamics. The residual density has a trapezoidal section and an exponential tail. The dresidual, presidual, and qresidual functions receive their distribution parameters through the param vector. The ordinary Hawkes model is the special case with an exponential residual distribution of rate 1. Use set_residual to wrap the distribution functions with log-density and tail-probability support.

mu1_d <- 0.5; alpha1_d <- 1; beta1_d <- 1.2; a <- 0.7; ell <- 1.6
hspec1_d <- set_residual(
  new("hspec", mu = mu1_d, alpha = alpha1_d, beta = beta1_d),
  param = c(a = a, ell = ell),
  dresidual = dtzexp, presidual = ptzexp,
  qresidual = qtzexp, rresidual = rtzexp
)
dh1_real <- hsim(hspec1_d, size = 3000)
hist(
  dh1_real$inter_arrival[dh1_real$inter_arrival < 3],
  breaks = 50,
  main = "Histogram of Inter-Arrival Times",
  xlab = "Inter-Arrival Time",
  ylab = "Frequency"
)

Use logLik to evaluate the observed inter-arrival times under hspec1_d. Setting infer = TRUE also returns the intensity and residual processes in infer_res_dh1.

# Infer the residual process using the log-likelihood method
# 'infer_res_dh1' contains the inferred process data based on the inter-arrival times
infer_res_dh1 <- logLik(hspec1_d, inter_arrival = dh1_real$inter_arrival, infer = TRUE)

# Plot a histogram of the inferred residual process
hist(
  infer_res_dh1$res_process1,
  breaks = 100,
  probability = TRUE,
  main = "Histogram of Inferred Residual Process",
  xlab = "Residual Value",
  ylab = "Density"
)

x <- seq(0, 8, 0.1)

lines(
  x,
  dtzexp(x, a = a, ell = ell),
  col = 'red',
  lwd = 2
)

# Add legend for clarity
legend("topright", legend = "Theoretical PDF", col = "red", lwd = 2)

Two-dimensional model

The same approach extends to multiple dimensions, using parameter matrices as in a multivariate Hawkes model.

mu2_d <- matrix(c(0.3), nrow = 2)
alpha2_d <- matrix(c(0.5, 0.8, 0.8, 0.5), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
beta2_d <- matrix(c(1.5, 1.5, 1.5, 1.5), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
a <- 0.7; ell <- 1.6

hspec2_du <- set_residual(
  new("hspec", mu = mu2_d, alpha = alpha2_d, beta = beta2_d),
  param = c(a = a, ell = ell),
  dresidual = dtzexp, presidual = ptzexp,
  qresidual = qtzexp, rresidual = rtzexp
)
print(hspec2_du)

The following histogram shows inter-arrival times from a model with tzexp residuals.

set.seed(1107)
duh2_real <- hsim(hspec2_du, size = 10000)
# Plot a histogram of the inter-arrival times less than 5
hist(
  duh2_real$inter_arrival[duh2_real$inter_arrival < 5],
  breaks = 50,
  main = "Histogram of Inter-Arrival Times",
  xlab = "Inter-Arrival Time",
  ylab = "Frequency"
)

Use logLik with infer = TRUE to recover the intensity and residual processes.

infer_res_dh2 <- logLik(hspec2_du, 
                        inter_arrival = duh2_real$inter_arrival, 
                        type = duh2_real$type, infer = TRUE)

Under a correctly specified model, the inferred residuals follow the specified residual distribution.

# Plot a histogram of the inferred residual process
hist(
  infer_res_dh2$res_process2,
  breaks = 50,
  probability = TRUE,
  main = "Histogram of Inferred Residual Process",
  xlab = "Residual Value",
  ylab = "Density"
)

# Generate a sequence of x values for plotting the theoretical distribution
x <- seq(0, 8, 0.1)

# Add a line to the histogram representing the theoretical density function
lines(
  x,
  dtzexp(x, a = a, ell = ell),
  col = 'red',
  lwd = 2
)

# Add legend for clarity
legend("topright", legend = "Theoretical PDF", col = "red", lwd = 2)

The transformed residuals in eres_process1 follow an exponential distribution with rate 1 under a correctly specified model.

hist(
  infer_res_dh2$eres_process1,
  breaks = 50,
  probability = TRUE,
  main = "Histogram of Inferred eResidual Process",
  xlab = "Residual Value",
  ylab = "Density"

x <- seq(0, 8, 0.1)

# Add a line to the histogram representing the theoretical density function
lines(
  x,
  dexp(x),
  col = 'red',
  lwd = 2
)

# Add legend for clarity
legend("topright", legend = "Theoretical PDF", col = "red", lwd = 2)

Use hfit for maximum likelihood estimation. The distribution requires 0 < a <= 3, ell > 0, and a nonnegative density. The last condition is nonlinear, so the custom objective below checks each candidate with dtzexp and returns -Inf when the distribution is invalid.

residual_loglik <- function(object, inter_arrival, type, param) {
  valid <- tryCatch({
    dtzexp(1, a = param["a"], ell = param["ell"])
    TRUE
  }, error = function(e) FALSE)
  if (!valid) return(-Inf)
  suppressMessages(logLik(object, inter_arrival = inter_arrival, type = type))
}
constraints <- list(
  ineqA = rbind(diag(6), c(0, 0, 0, 0, -1, 0)),
  ineqB = c(rep(0, 6), 3)
)
mle_dh <- hfit(hspec2_du, 
               inter_arrival = duh2_real$inter_arrival, 
               type = duh2_real$type,
               mylogLik = residual_loglik,
               constraints = constraints)
#> hfit: equal starting values within each matrix share a parameter (reduced = TRUE; mu, alpha, beta).
#> Use reduced = FALSE to estimate matrix entries separately.
summary(mle_dh)

Hawkes curvature stabilization does not change this custom FRPP objective. The moving transition point of tzexp can make numerical Hessians step dependent. A successful optimizer return code does not validate the reported Wald standard errors. See the fit diagnostic report for the one-sided derivative and profile checks.

These constraints keep the six parameters nonnegative and enforce a <= 3, the upper limit of the trapezoid-exponential distribution. The parameter order is mu1, alpha1.1, alpha1.2, beta1.1, a, and ell.

Reconstruction also updates the residual density, distribution, quantile, and generator functions with the shared estimates of a and ell. The custom objective and optimization constraints remain part of the fitting step; logLik() evaluates the restored model’s residual-distribution likelihood.

estimated_dh <- fitted_hspec(mle_dh)
initial_dh <- fit_initial_state(mle_dh)
formals(estimated_dh@rresidual)$param
#>         a       ell 
#> 0.7181419 1.6378856
inferred_dh <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = estimated_dh,
  inter_arrival = duh2_real$inter_arrival, type = duh2_real$type, infer = TRUE), initial_dh))
c(fitted = as.numeric(logLik(mle_dh)), restored = inferred_dh$loglikelihood)
#>    fitted  restored 
#> -12407.47 -12407.47

The following example uses a uniform residual distribution on [0,2][0, 2].


#set.seed(117)
mu2_d <- matrix(c(0.5), nrow = 2)
alpha2_d <- matrix(c(0.3, 0.3, 0.3, 0.3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
beta2_d <- matrix(c(1.2, 1.2, 1.2, 1.2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)

hspec2_du <- new("hspec", mu=mu2_d, alpha=alpha2_d, beta=beta2_d,
                 rresidual = function(size) runif(n=size, 0, 2),
                 dresidual = function(x, param = numeric(0), log = FALSE)
                   dunif(x, 0, 2, log = log),
                 presidual = function(q, param = numeric(0), lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)
                   punif(q, 0, 2, lower.tail = lower.tail, log.p = log.p),
                 qresidual = function(p, param = numeric(0), lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)
                   qunif(p, 0, 2, lower.tail = lower.tail, log.p = log.p))

duh2_real <- hsim(hspec2_du, size = 5000)

Plot a histogram of the inferred residuals:


infer_res_duh2 <- logLik(hspec2_du, 
                         inter_arrival = duh2_real$inter_arrival, 
                         type = duh2_real$type, infer = TRUE)

hist(
  infer_res_duh2$res_process1,
  breaks = 50,
  probability = TRUE,
  main = "Histogram of Inferred Residual Process",
  xlab = "Residual Value",
  ylab = "Density"
)
